title: NoSQL Modeling
description: Learn data modeling patterns for document, key-value, wide-column, and graph databases in production systems.

data.text: NoSQL data modeling looks very different from relational design. Instead of normalizing data into related tables, you embed or reference related entities based on access patterns. The guiding principle is simple: design your data model around the queries your application will run, not around a universal normalized structure.

Document databases like MongoDB store related data together in JSON-like documents. Embed nested objects when the child data is always accessed with the parent, and use references when the child is shared across many parents. Embedding avoids joins but creates duplication; referencing keeps data normalized but requires multiple lookups.

data.title: Document sizing
data.text: MongoDB documents are limited to 16 MB. Avoid embedding unbounded arrays like comments or log entries. Use references for one-to-many relationships where the many side can grow without limit.

Key-value stores like Redis and DynamoDB are the simplest NoSQL model. The application serializes the entire value object, and the database stores it as a blob. Queries are by primary key only. This makes key-value stores ideal for caching, session data, shopping carts, and feature flags. Design your keys carefully because secondary queries are not supported.

Wide-column stores like Cassandra organize data into column families. Each row has a partition key that determines which node stores the data, and clustering columns that control on-disk sorting. Model your tables around the queries you need. A single Cassandra table can replace multiple SQL tables if you design the primary key to match your query pattern.

data.caption: NoSQL access patterns drive data modeling
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[Application query] --> B{Query pattern?}
    B -->|By user + date| C[Document store: embed]
    B -->|By key only| D[Key-value: serialize blob]
    B -->|By partition + range| E[Wide-column: composite key]
    B -->|By relationship| F[Graph: traverse edges]

data.text: Graph databases like Neo4j model entities as nodes and relationships as edges. They excel when your domain is inherently connected: social networks, recommendation engines, fraud detection, or knowledge graphs. Traversing relationships in a graph database is O(degree) while the same operation in SQL requires recursive CTEs that slow down with depth.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Design NoSQL models around query patterns, not universal normalization.
Embed documents when child data is always read with the parent; reference when it is shared.
Key-value stores need carefully chosen keys because queries are limited to primary key lookups.
Wide-column and graph databases require deep understanding of access patterns before writing data.
